modules.title: Sources, authority, and careful claims
objectives: Distinguish canon, institutional teaching, commentary, and historical evidence.
State a doctrinal claim with a source and a limit.
modules.lesson: Studying doctrine begins with identifying the kind of claim being made. A passage can be canonical, a statement can represent current institutional teaching, and a book can offer useful commentary without all three having the same function. A historical record may tell us what someone taught at a particular time without settling what the Church teaches today. Keep four fields beside every note: claim, source, setting, and confidence. Ask whether your wording is broader than the evidence. “This passage teaches…” is often more defensible than “Every Latter-day Saint believes…”. This course assesses your ability to understand and explain teachings; it does not assess personal belief or religious worthiness. Start a source ledger now. You will revise it as new evidence changes how precisely you can express a claim.

readings.prompt: Which topics belong to the opening four articles, and which questions do they leave unanswered?
readings.answerGuide: Identify Godhead, individual accountability, Christ’s Atonement, and foundational principles and ordinances; avoid treating a compact summary as a complete theology.
readings.completion: Respond to the reading prompt with a claim and a reference. Reviewer checks the answer guide; clicking or merely opening a resource earns no XP.

practices.prompt: Classify a scripture passage, a conference address, a historical diary, and a devotional book.
practices.successCriteria: Give each a source type, explain its appropriate use, and avoid an automatic authority ranking based only on the author’s title.

modules.title: The Godhead and the language of unity
objectives: Explain the LDS distinction between unity and identity.
Represent Nicene belief without caricature.
modules.lesson: Theological words are useful only when their meanings are made explicit. In Latter-day Saint teaching, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are distinct, while their work and purpose are united. Read statements about their unity beside passages that distinguish them. Do not turn “one” into a single definition that must apply in every context. When comparing this teaching with Nicene Christianity, ask how each tradition uses person, being, substance, and unity. Nicene belief is not simply the idea that God changes masks; that description confuses the Trinity with modalism. A good first explanation stays close to its own sources and admits where ordinary analogies break down. Make a two-column glossary: what a source says, and the meaning you are assigning to its words.

readings.prompt: What distinctions does this passage make, and what does it not explain?
readings.answerGuide: Identify the Father and Son as having bodies and the Holy Ghost as a personage of spirit; do not infer an exhaustive account of divine metaphysics.

modules.title: Evidence, genre, and historical claim testing
objectives: Match evidence to the kind of claim.

modules.lesson: Documents can support claims without supporting every claim made about them. modules.lesson: A concept map is strongest when its arrows say something specific. Replace vague connections with relationships such as grounds, invites, qualifies, or creates tension with. modules.title: Charity, disagreement, and pastoral case analysis
objectives: Apply doctrine without claiming authority over private lives.

modules.lesson: A well-argued position can still be expressed in a way that harms dialogue. Charity is not the avoidance of every disagreement; it includes how people are represented and treated while ideas are examined. A doctrinal explanation should not become an unearned diagnosis of a person’s motives, spiritual status, or mental health. modules.title: Teaching responsibly and correcting mistakes
objectives: Create a source-transparent learning experience.
Revise teaching after finding a factual or interpretive error.
modules.lesson: Teaching turns your interpretation into someone else’s starting point. A responsible lesson therefore makes its sources and limitations visible. Choose a learning objective that can actually be assessed, use enough context for the reader to evaluate a claim, and include an alternative interpretation when it is relevant. Avoid manufacturing certainty to make a lesson feel inspiring. When you discover an error, correct the content and explain the change plainly. A correction is part of scholarship rather than evidence that learning has failed. Accessibility also matters: a learner should be able to complete the objective without purchasing a book, watching an unavailable video, or disclosing private religious experiences. Build the lesson around understanding that can be demonstrated in several forms.

modules.title: Capstone revision and an ongoing scholar’s practice
objectives: Revise accurately in response to critique.
Produce a transferable, accessible teaching artifact.
modules.lesson: Sage is a milestone in a learning path, not a certificate of religious authority. The final project demonstrates that you can integrate sources, reason fairly, and communicate responsibly. Ask a reviewer to identify the weakest claim, the least clear term, and the alternative you have represented least adequately. Revise those points before polishing the presentation. Provide an accessible summary for a newcomer and a transparent bibliography for a specialist. Keep an errata section and a list of questions for future study. Mature scholarship does not end with a tier badge: it continues through correction, better evidence, and more careful listening. The final assessment therefore values limitations and revision alongside accuracy and a coherent thesis.

capstone.title: A sourced LDS doctrinal synthesis
formats: 20–30-minute presentation with written outline and source notes
Accessible equivalent approved against the same rubric
requirements: One bounded research question and a defensible thesis.
At least 10 substantively used sources, including at least 4 canonical selections and 2 current LDS institutional sources.

At least 1 historical primary source and 1 source representing a comparison tradition when relevant to the chosen question; otherwise explain why they are not relevant and substitute an appropriate academic or documentary source.
Identify perspective and claim type; do not treat an institutional essay as independent scholarly consensus.
One serious alternative reading or objection, answered or used to narrow the thesis.
One fictional practical or teaching application.
A claim-level citation trail, annotated bibliography, revision log, accessible newcomer summary, and at least 3 explicit limitations or open questions.
Use only original writing, approved app scripture rendering, links, and rights-cleared materials.
capstone.review: A qualified human reviewer or a validated assessment workflow must evaluate the rubric. Self-checking completion does not constitute a pass. A course facilitator should have documented familiarity with LDS doctrine, source criticism, and respectful cross-tradition comparison.

rubric.title: Accuracy and context
descriptors: Major distortions or unsupported doctrinal claims.
Mostly accurate but important context missing.
Accurate, contextual account with minor gaps.
Precise account with context and clearly qualified limits.

rubric.title: Traceable sources
descriptors: Some sources but unclear attribution or inappropriate support.
Major claims traceable to appropriate sources.
Claim-level trail distinguishes perspectives, settings, and limits.

rubric.title: Fair alternative
descriptors: No serious alternative, or a caricature.
Serious alternative represented and reasonably answered.
Strong alternative used to test and improve the thesis.

rubric.title: Coherent synthesis and limitations
descriptors: Incoherent argument or no meaningful synthesis.
Recognizable thesis but weak integration or missing limits.
Coherent synthesis with practical application and explicit limits.
Well-integrated, accessible synthesis with responsible application and a clear revision trail.
